      My net NFTs on Sepolia

      How it works
      1. Cast a net. Before nets close at 21:00 UTC (22:00 your time). A net is a test NFT on Sepolia One net per wallet per night. Nobody picks a hamster.
      2. He runs. Squeektoshi is a real hamster. Squeekchain measures his wheel every 10 minutes and settles it on-chain (Sepolia). His run sets up the quantum program: each round tilts a quantum coin, a lazy round barely, a sprint all the way.
      3. The chip drops 4,000 times. After his night ends (12:00 UTC, 13:00 your time) a real IBM quantum computer runs his program 4,000 times. Each run is one drop: it lands on one of the 16 hamsters.
      4. One drop is yours. Your net gets one of those 4,000 drops, drawn at random on-chain once the night's result is posted, so nobody can choose it or know it before. The hamster it landed on is your catch. The fewer drops a hamster gets, the rarer it is. If your drop is chip noise (a spot he could not reach that night, or one with under 1% of the drops), your hamster got away.
      Commonthe rest
      Uncommon3rd + 4th fewest
      Rare2nd fewest
      Epicthe fewest
      LegendaryEpic + first look

      The least-visited spot he could reach is Epic; if the chip's very first look landed there, it is Legendary.

      The ring

      Each of the 16 spots has its own hamster: the spot's 4 bits pick a party hat, glasses, a scarf and a grin. The ring turns with his night: he starts at his own spot, his total turns counted round the ring of 16 (the dashed ring on the wheel). Each step moves him one spot, so he can only land on every other spot, and on a short night only near his start: the rest of the ring is out of reach that night (greyed). Drops that land there are the chip's noise: a net whose drop lands there gets away. Where he starts depends on his total turns, so nobody knows it before he runs.

      A normal computer can simulate this small walk. What is real: his run is real, and the chip is a real IBM quantum computer with real noise.

      The recipe in 6 lines

      1. Read his turns per active 10-minute round from SqueekCore roundPage on Sepolia (12:00 to 12:00 UTC).
      2. One step per round. Too many rounds: even groups, mean turns rounded half up (at most 16 steps up to 4 Nov, recipe v1.1; at most 10 from 5 Nov, recipe v1.2, which also runs with noise protection).
      3. Coin tilt = π × min(turns, 700) / 700 (an RY turn of the coin qubit).
      4. Start at his own spot: total turns mod 16. Coin (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2. Each step: tilt the coin, then coin 1 steps +1, coin 0 steps −1, on a ring of 16.
      5. IBM runs it 4,000 times. A spot is in reach that night if (spot + total turns + steps) is even and it is at most as many spots from his start as he took steps; out of reach: he got away. A spot in reach with at least 1% of the landings is caught; rank those by landings: the fewest is Epic (Legendary if the chip's very first shot landed there), the next Rare, the two after that Uncommon, the rest Common. The spot's 4 bits pick the looks.
      6. Each net gets one of the night's landings: keccak256 of (the night, the posted result's hash and job id, the net's token id) modulo the number of landings, counted off spot by spot from spot 0. If that spot is caught, the net catches its hamster with its rank; if not (out of reach, or under 1%), the drop was chip noise and the net got away.

      Proof stamp: the twin test

      Each chip job also plays a card game with two linked qubits that cannot talk. Any fixed plan wins at most 75% of rounds.

      Play it yourself: can a plan beat 75%?

      Each round, twin A and twin B each get a card, FUR or HAT, and answer 0 or 1 without seeing the other's card. They win if they answer the same, except when both got HAT: then they must answer differently. Give them a fixed plan (tap an answer to flip it):

      Squeektoshi is a real hamster. Probably the first hamster to program a quantum computer.

      Squeektoshi's wheel runs are measured by Squeekchain and settled on Sepolia in 10-minute rounds. His night becomes a quantum walk on a ring of 16 spots, and IBM's chip looks where he lands. Test tokens only (Sepolia test ETH, Squeekchain test SQK): nothing here has money value.

      A normal computer can simulate this small walk. What is real is that every chip result shown here ran on real IBM hardware, with real noise, on his real run.
